details: Problem
Unify provider quotation and issuance flows across motor, medical, group medical and fire insurance.
My ownership

Built rate-fetching and normalization, then led development and operations as Engineering Director. Held final architectural decision authority, evaluating approaches against integration constraints, available resources and commercial requirements. Explained trade-offs to stakeholders and generally sought informed consensus.
Key Engineering Decision

Designed an event-driven quotation architecture using Node.js. Introduced quotation caching and pre-warmed data to reduce repeated processing and support faster quotations, including potential renewals for existing customers.
Evidence

Historical production analytics recorded real-user activity. I recall a peak of approximately 15,000 distinct users within one hour; the original dashboard is not available for independent corroboration. This is an approximate historical recollection, not a concurrency, request-throughput or load-test measurement.
Business rules

Quotations expire after seven days. Changes to customer information that affect quotation terms require quotation revision. Caching and pre-warming do not exempt quotations from these validity requirements.
Constraints & approach

Integrated insurer APIs and internal services under changing business and regulatory requirements. Applied security and consistency checks; modernised legacy code for clarity and integration stability.
Delivered Capability

Supported real-time mass quotations with rate normalization and integrated issuance for consumers, large commercial clients, internal teams and partners, while accommodating expiry and changes affecting quotations.

content.name: Multilingual portfolio engineering
content.problem: Maintain one professional source across eleven languages, scripts and reading directions.
content.role: I own the route model, content boundaries, presentation controls and localization maintenance workflow.
content.decision: Keep canonical English strings and one locale registry; isolate professional Q&A from translation.
content.result: Eleven registered locales share localized routes, metadata, translation notices and static HTML generation.
content.focus: Direction-aware layouts, accessible controls and incremental translation provenance. Automated checks do not establish linguistic fluency or replace native-language and screen-reader review.
narrative: One registry, one content workflow
Localization pipeline
Canonical English → AST string extraction
Incremental translation → source hashes and provenance
Catalog validation → coverage and editorial review
Lazy locale catalogs → static localized routes and metadata

React and i18next use languages.json for locale order, direction, fonts, calendars and writing modes. URL, saved preference, browser preference and English fallback resolve language in that order. Switching preserves route, query and fragment.

Extraction, validation, coverage and prerendering are scripted. Translation sync requires configured authoring credentials; new case-study translations were generated directly by the coding assistant. They are machine-translated and await fluent editorial review.

Every non-English page retains the localized disclosure near navigation and a matching English-original link. Canonical URLs are locale-specific; reciprocal hreflang links and x-default connect equivalent pages. Translation is performed during authoring, never from visitor conversations.
Adaptive Preferences Across Scripts and Layouts

Hidden language and display menus made global preferences harder to discover. The utility rail exposes five controls while reusing the existing preference services; its own state only manages disclosures.

One nonmodal panel opens at a time. Focus enters the panel without a trap; Escape and Close return it to the trigger. Navigation and outside clicks dismiss it. Detailed controls load on demand, with a retry action if loading fails.

Logical docking places the rail on the right in LTR and left in Arabic. Compact screens use an expandable Settings entry. Controls remain horizontal in vertical CJK mode; saved indicators synchronize after hydration. Language switching preserves route, query and fragment.

Privacy UI reuses existing consent state: opening a panel does not enable analytics. DNT/GPC suppression remains separate from saved consent. Keyboard, locale and automated accessibility checks support the implementation; screen-reader, physical-device and fluent translation review remain pending.
Arabic utility rail with the language panel open on the left.
Local implementation capture: Arabic RTL docking and a horizontal language panel.
Inspect the portfolio source
Inspect the evidence
A deliberate English-only boundary

PACE-RAG professional questions, answers and evidence remain English-only. Its region retains lang=en, dir=ltr, translate=no and horizontal writing. Surrounding notices are localized; changing locale preserves the assistant and conversation state.

Font fallbacks, text scaling, reduced motion and RTL are presentation responsibilities. Automated browser checks support regression detection; native-language review, physical-device coverage and actual screen-reader sessions remain separate work.

projects.name: NAAE

content.name: NAAE
content.problem: Make a scene recognizable at a distance while preserving meaningful narrative characters up close.
content.role: I directed the visual language, rendering constraints and iterative review of the procedural engine.
content.decision: Reserve exact narrative text before allocating semantic glyph texture; separate occupancy from intensity.
content.result: Saved Organic v0.3 and Pixel-Hybrid v0.4 artifacts expose configuration and integrity diagnostics.
content.focus: Seeded geometry, source integrity and bounded character budgets. Scene mode is experimental; physical print quality and official release dates are unverified.
narrative: An artifact-backed evolution

The canonical project name is Narrative ASCII Art Engine. Local documentation describes v0.1 object allocation and v0.2 layered landscapes. Saved v0.2, v0.3 and v0.4 outputs support the comparisons below; no Git history or tags were available to establish release dates.
Protect the story, then compose the texture
Artwork generation pipeline
Seeded scene graph → layered geometry and spatial regions
Physical budget → exact narrative allocation and source indices
Eligible cells → coverage, semantic glyphs and independent intensity
Integrity diagnostics → SVG text, PNG and scene configuration

Coverage counts visibly occupied eligible cells; protected narrative spaces are excluded. Intensity controls appearance independently of occupancy. Pixel-Hybrid adds stepped geometry and tile-coherent glyph selection while sharing narrative protection. Diagnostics are engineering checks, not aesthetic quality scores.

The studio/package v0.4 label is separate from rendererVersion: Organic uses 0.3.0; Pixel-Hybrid uses 0.4.0. Scene mode is experimental. Supported text is measured Latin ASCII; physical print quality and a public studio release are pending.
Engineering the Visual Identity: From Narrative Landscapes to Glyph-Based Portraits

A portrait needs recognizable facial structure at a distance and authentic characters up close. Early tonal adjustments could not recover detail missing from the source grid. The portfolio reconstruction therefore works on an existing glyph SVG, not directly on a photograph.

Build-time analysis samples glyph luminance at three neighborhood scales. Font-calibrated ink coverage and local gradients guide bounded size and shape variants while preserving the character sequence. This is source-field analysis, not facial-landmark detection; it cannot invent missing anatomy.

Dark-mode amber supports luminous strokes. Light-mode glyph experiments needed separate ink palettes, tonal mappings and reduced background competition; bright eye highlights and pale small glyphs exposed the limits of palette changes. The current homepage selects a separate illustration in light mode and the reconstructed glyph SVG in dark mode.
Dark homepage with an amber glyph portrait in the narrative landscape.
Local dark treatment: actual SVG characters, reconstructed before runtime.
Light homepage with a separate illustrated portrait in the landscape.
Local light treatment: a separate illustration, not an ASCII portrait.

Deterministic reconstruction and geometry tests make the transformation inspectable. These portfolio-specific experiments do not establish standalone NAAE photo support. The captures show current treatments, not a historical before/after benchmark; identity recognition and deployed parity are not independently established.
Inspect the portfolio source
Inspect the evidence
The Unmapped Path: narrative typography for recovery

The 404 scene applies the same visual language to a useful failure state: seeded SVG-text ridges and a vanishing trail support a localized explanation, quote and recovery links. Compact screens receive a separate composition; decorative glyphs remain hidden from assistive technology.

Static localized fallback documents preserve recovery without JavaScript. Recorded local Pages checks returned HTTP 404 for missing paths and 200 for known routes; this is local hosting evidence, not live deployment verification. The artwork is distinct from the homepage and imports no studio engine.

An extensible simulation with AI.
How I used AI-assisted development to build an office narrative game, applying human judgment and engineering expertise to turn repeated feedback into a system I could keep extending.

Executive summary / Independent engineering project
Challenge
Build an extensible office simulation where technical work, conversations and spatial interactions have connected consequences.
Role
I directed the product and architecture, set engineering constraints, reviewed AI-assisted implementation and iterated through playtesting.
A TypeScript simulation owns state; React presents the interface and Phaser handles spatial presentation. Validated saves, migrations and headless verification support change.
Inspect the boundaries
Engineering decisions
Separate state ownership from rendering, reproduce recorded actions deterministically, preserve supported historical saves and require evidence for each bounded iteration.
Review the workflow

The 15 October 2026 campaign against the recorded 0.3.0-rc.1 / monday-8 snapshot verified 112,402 completed simulation runs and independently replayed 8,050 retained artifacts. It verified 44 ending targets; two campaign target gaps remained.
Read the scope and gaps
Limitations

Historical campaign figures are not current game-wide totals or evidence of the hosted build. Automated traversal does not establish human understanding, enjoyment, browser accessibility or production infrastructure scale.
Check the evidence sources
Give each layer a clear responsibility.

The game uses TypeScript, React, Phaser 3 and Vite. Its simulation owns the world state and publishes snapshots. React subscribes to those snapshots for interface updates; Phaser handles spatial presentation and traversal. A bridge carries room, proximity and interaction signals between the office and the interface.

This boundary lets the simulation run without rendering the office. It supports deterministic tests, automated traversal and save-restoration checks, while interface and artwork changes can be inspected separately. Shared state still needs care: the main simulation runtime coordinates many systems, and adding a module is not free of integration work.

Persistence
Validated snapshots, migrations and local archives

Tests, traversal and independent replay
Responsibility diagram simplified from the runtime, UI subscriptions and game bridge. It shows engineering boundaries without disclosing narrative rules.
Extend content through explicit rules

Authored registries, typed actions and state predicates give new content a defined integration point. The event Director filters and scores authored possibilities; it is not a runtime language model inventing the story.
Seeded randomness makes a recorded sequence reproducible under matching code and settings. That is useful for debugging; it does not make the whole possibility space exhaustively tested.
Keep optional work out of startup

The game defers Phaser, optional panels and other modules. Bundle checks inspect the startup graph and enforce size budgets, including keeping the analytics SDK outside startup until optional consent.
These controls make growth measurable. They do not establish a universal frame-rate or mobile performance guarantee.
Preserve progress while the system evolves

Save loading validates the record and applies explicit incremental migrations. Supported historical saves receive conservative defaults; loading restores a snapshot without replaying gameplay. Original bytes are retained before browser conversion, and unsupported or unreadable records have recovery paths.
Diagram 04 / Save compatibility
Invalid or unsupported records are preserved for recovery. Browser origin, storage access and quota remain real constraints; local saves are not cloud sync.
Eight hours of automated exploration.

The latest reviewed completion campaign ran on 15 October 2026 against a recorded 0.3.0-rc.1 / monday-8 source snapshot. Its eight-hour execution budget produced 112,402 completed simulation runs with matching verified receipts and unique run identifiers. The integrity report passed.

The tool used witness-guided exploration through normal simulation actions, with recorded settings and source identity. Of the retained artifacts, 8,050 were independently replayed. A compact suite selected 44 replay witnesses covering 118 observed targets. Those targets mix endings, achievements and challenges; they are not 118 separate stories.
How the CLI turns timelines into reviewable evidence.
The developer-only

CLI exercises the real simulation through legal inputs. It records the order of decisions and semantic state changes, rather than treating every seed or wording change as a new story. That gives me evidence for deciding which variations deserve a closer playtest and which missing paths need investigation.
Diagram 05 / From story traversal to gameplay review
Timeline variants
Compare ordered, meaningful decisions and state changes. Cosmetic wording and seed-only differences do not create separate route identities.
Essential variations
Inspect distinct verified route families and canonical prerequisites. A frequent event in sampled runs is an association, not proof that the event is necessary.
Blocking states and gaps
Distinguish unmet prerequisites, legitimate refusals and stalled attempts from replay failures or a search that exhausted its budget. An unobserved path is not proven impossible.
Human review → a focused revision or playtest

I can inspect retained timelines, compare counterfactual branches and prioritise suspected bottlenecks. The reports provide investigation leads; they do not rewrite the game or establish that a variation is enjoyable. Any change still needs a clear brief, regression checks and human evaluation.

The campaign ended at its duration budget with two target gaps: the unverified outcome above and its associated achievement. That is an unresolved verification gap, not proof that the outcome is impossible. A long run is useful precisely because it can expose a stubborn blind spot rather than manufacture an all-green coverage claim.

Headless traversal does not exercise room collision, visual layout, keyboard focus or whether a person enjoys the pacing. Those need browser checks and human playtests. The 15 October release notes separately record 733 automated tests and a 133-test save-compatibility gate for the prepared release candidate; these are historical release checks, not tests rerun by this case study.
Collect evidence about understanding, not just completion.

The crawl records deterministic actions, semantic changes and verification receipts so I can investigate the system’s behaviour. Human playtesting answers different questions: did someone understand the next task, recognise the result of a choice or know why a puzzle attempt failed? The game’s optional analytics is designed to support those questions alongside direct feedback.
Implemented playtest instrumentation and the questions it can support
Collected signals
Question for review
Interpretation limit
Puzzle views, attempts, repeated wrong plans, hints and active time
Does a viewed stage receive an attempt? Where might instructions or feedback need attention?
A long visit or repeated attempt can mean deliberation, difficulty or confusion; the metric alone cannot tell which.
Presented events, committed choices, consequence receipts and ordered run context
What did the player encounter, choose and observe before the next decision?
Recorded sequence and linked consequences do not prove that the player noticed or understood them.
Run milestones, completions, resumes, replay activity and active/paused timing
Where was a run last observed, and how does a repeat visit differ from an initial run?
Missing completion is not confirmed abandonment. Pauses, later returns, consent changes and delivery gaps matter.

Gameplay sharing is consent-gated and uses explicit event/property allowlists. Automatic click capture and session replay are disabled in the game’s adapter. Local run records and diagnostic exports serve a separate purpose; a playtest report is copied or downloaded explicitly rather than automatically submitted.

No private player records or live analytics results are published here. These are implemented collection capabilities, not a claim that player behaviour has already established a particular improvement. I still need to inspect the evidence, ask players what they understood and evaluate any revision in context.
AI accelerated the work. Expertise guided the decisions.

AI made it practical to move quickly between a feature idea, implementation and a diagnostic tool. My responsibility was to decide what the game should become, recognise where the result fell short and make the next change reviewable. Human involvement mattered at every stage: setting priorities, interpreting feedback and deciding what evidence was sufficient for the question being asked.

The value of domain expertise was in turning observations into durable requirements. Ambiguous choices called for clearer feedback. Evolving systems needed boundaries and save compatibility. Generated artwork needed visual inspection and reliable extraction. Automated traversal could verify recorded behaviour at scale, while pacing, clarity and the experience of playing still needed human evaluation.

I would carry that approach into another project: define acceptance criteria early, preserve observations alongside decisions, and evaluate each change at the appropriate layer. Better prompts emerged from understanding the product and its constraints. The outcome I am aiming for is maintainable behaviour and a coherent player experience.

How these numbers were counted
01 / The product problem
A small office. A growing system.

No Two Mondays starts with a simple premise: one working day, three coworkers and a production outage. The challenge was to make decisions feel connected across technical work, conversations and the office around you. The setting could stay compact while the underlying system became richer.

I used Codex throughout development, directing features, playing the results, reporting what felt wrong and asking for focused revisions. My work included setting the product constraints, deciding which changes belonged in the game, and requiring evidence that new work preserved existing behaviour.

Here, scalability means being able to add and revise behaviour without losing consistency, save compatibility or a usable browser experience. This is a client-side game; the project does not demonstrate multiplayer concurrency or backend traffic scaling.

I wanted the characters to sound like people carrying their work into an ordinary conversation. These are authored in-game coffee responses, shown as separate excerpts rather than one exchange. They give a taste of the office humour without revealing incident explanations or story outcomes.
02 / Working with AI
The prompt started the work. Human judgment steered it.

Codex accelerated implementation, but each change still needed a human decision about what belonged in the game and whether the result worked. I set the direction, played the results, identified what felt unclear or inconsistent, and turned those observations into focused revisions. Keeping a human in the loop meant shaping the work throughout development: framing the problem, inspecting the result and deciding what needed to change.

Domain expertise made that feedback actionable. Software engineering knowledge helped me translate a feature request into requirements for state ownership, persistence, compatibility and regression checks. Interaction decisions needed a different lens: could a player understand a choice, notice its consequences and navigate the interface comfortably? The useful brief connected the intended experience to the constraints and evidence needed to evaluate it.
Diagram 01 / The development loop
Each review feeds the next brief. This is a synthesis of the recorded workflow, rather than a transcript of one session.
What I directed
Product scope, interaction clarity, engineering constraints and acceptance criteria. I judged the results against the intended experience and directed follow-up changes.
What AI accelerated
Implementation, test scaffolding, diagnostic tools, documentation and asset iteration. I used those outputs as material to inspect, test and refine.
03 / The cost of iteration
210 prompts did not mean 210 finished features.

The historical audit recovered 210 deduplicated human prompts across 20 interactive sessions. A union of its bug-fixing, refinement and refactoring tags contains 37 distinct prompts. The project feedback log separately records 21 feedback entries at the time of this review. These are different measures: a feedback entry may summarize several requests, and a prompt may address several concerns.

The tagging is automated and lexical. It describes the requests that were recovered, rather than proving how many code modifications were necessary or how much time each feature took. The audit is a partial historical record, not the total lifetime prompt count.

Art and animation took repeated correction.

Getting the character art right took several rounds of direction and visual review. I asked for changes to the player’s proportions and facial treatment, then had to preserve that approved likeness across different directions and walking poses. I preferred the original, unnormalised artwork; the generation notes record that preference alongside the extraction and registration requirements.

Walking exposed problems that a still image could hide. Equal-sized frame cells did not guarantee equal visible character sizes, and the earlier sequence mixed walking contacts with idle and blink poses. The correction work separated those states, used a uniform scale per character and tied animation to measured movement. A live check also caught gait resets between fixed-step physics updates. These were asset and runtime problems that needed different checks.

The art review still records subtle support-leg differences in some generated poses, including Maya’s front passing frames. Automated bounds, registration and sequence checks could verify parts of the asset contract; they could not establish convincing anatomical motion on their own. I needed to inspect the artwork and movement in the game, and the remaining pose limitations were kept explicit.
From early visuals to the current build.

These retained development captures show the early presentation, the character remaster, its sizing/walking correction and the latest reviewed environment redesign. Here, v1–v3 label historical visual milestones, not game release numbers. The latest entry shows the local build captured on 15 October 2026. The captures use different viewport sizes and are not a matched animation comparison. Select an image to inspect the original full-size capture.
Dialogue UI: from a reply to a decision with context.

The dialogue interface evolved alongside the feedback system. These selected captures show changes in hierarchy, reading space and the relationship between previous results and the next choice. They show routine office interruptions before a response is chosen; no incident explanation or story outcome is revealed. The latest image was captured from the current source on 15 October 2026.
Puzzle UI: make the plan readable before executing it.

The recovery puzzle separates available operations from the player’s proposed order. These historical and current captures keep the plan empty and the notes closed. They illustrate interface evolution, rather than three different solutions or new puzzle rules. I have omitted diagnosis logs, submitted plans and revealed hints so the reasoning stays in the game.

How the case study was grounded.

The prompt figures come from an existing local development audit of surviving Codex records. It deduplicates human messages and excludes machine-agent tasks from the human-prompt count. The 37-prompt figure is the distinct union of three overlapping workflow tags: bug fixing, refinement and refactoring. Classification is lexical and can miss or misclassify requests. Missing history and later development are outside that snapshot.

The revision examples come from the project feedback log, refinement notes and art review. Architecture was checked against the TypeScript simulation, React subscriptions, Phaser bridge, save migrations and bundle checks. Traversal figures come from the 15 October completion campaign’s coverage, integrity, checkpoint and replay-suite reports. Public locked labels were checked against the game’s hint registry.

Only aggregate evidence and spoiler-safe descriptions are reproduced here. Private chat transcripts, raw traversal traces, puzzle solutions, hidden conditions and real ending titles are not published.

A one-minute overview

PACE-RAG is a browser-first assistant for reviewed professional information, with a separate engineering Lab. Cached answers and deterministic technology lookups avoid hosted inference; other questions can use a locally loaded model to suggest relevant reviewed questions. Every direct answer retains its own validated sources.

Measured retrieval results below show how well expected answers appear in the ranked suggestions. They do not prove factual certainty or production readiness. Live generation, enterprise security and provider billing remain unverified; the public demo is experimental.
Architecture at a glance
Two paths share source validation. Technology relationships use confirmed facts; other wording uses retrieval.

The problem and constraints

Recruiters need concise answers supported by public sources. A free-tier-oriented design keeps reviewed answers and retrieval usable without hosted inference, provider quota or a live API. Browser inference trades a model download, CPU and memory for fewer remote dependencies; free-tier billing and production capacity have not been verified.
From query to evidence
Load a checksum-verified corpus and its versioned source and answer registries. Opening the assistant does not initialize the embedding model.

Exact reviewed questions reuse approved cached answers with their own citations. Bounded technology questions compose answers from owner-confirmed project facts using a directed ontology of entities, categories and relationships.

Other semantic queries initialize the pinned MiniLM q8 WASM model in a browser worker. Professional suggestions combine question-vector cosine, answer-body BM25 and bounded intent adjustments. Other Lab views retain reviewed-question-and-answer BM25. Distinct answer records are ranked once. Passage retrieval remains a separate evidence-discovery path.
Similarity suggests related questions; it does not establish answer equivalence. Unsupported requests abstain. Lexical retrieval and static sources remain available when model initialization fails.

Cached answers, technology composition and local retrieval make zero Workers AI inference calls. A guarded gateway exists in source, but live generation is disabled. Mocked quota/provider tests do not establish deployed runtime or billing behaviour.

Provenance and publication boundaries

Reuse requires current approval, matching source hash, document version, citation URL and corpus ownership. Professional Experience is isolated from implementation documentation and fictional test documents; scoped vector rows follow the same filtered records. Retrieved passages are labelled separately from sources supporting an answer.

Hash-bound owner publication approval covers the existing source and answer registries. Generated Q&A is never automatically promoted. Content changes need renewed review, and integrity or licensing failures block packaging. Historic professional snapshots retain their review context; the current portfolio clarifies ongoing WenSymes collaboration and the existence of this demonstration.

details: Problem
Staff needed to manage contracts, renewals, cancellations and financial visibility across more than 20 rental properties, including operational work outside the office.
My ownership
Designed and implemented the business subletting and home rental management system as a freelance Principal Full Stack Solution Developer.
Key Engineering Decision
Designed and developed a mobile-friendly, web-based rental management system to support operational work outside the office.
Domain design
Separated property, tenant and contract records to support multi-entity workflows, contract generation and payment tracking.
Operating constraints
Access described here is internet-connected through compatible mobile or desktop browsers.
Delivered Capability

Enabled access to property, tenant and rental records; supported rental contract renewals and sending contract PDFs directly from mobile devices. Staff could review rental and financial reports remotely, including property-level income, expenses and profit/loss. Supported rental operations involving more than 20 properties.

details: Business problem
Internal HR and operational administration needed to accommodate changing employee roles and organizational needs.
My ownership

Principal Full Stack Developer with final architectural decision authority for HR and administration tools. Evaluated viable approaches against available resources, stakeholder requirements and changing business processes, generally seeking informed consensus. The engagement continues as occasional professional collaboration.
Key Engineering Decision

Prioritized system flexibility so changing employee roles and responsibilities could be accommodated as organizational headcount and operational needs evolved. Designed modular service boundaries to support authenticated API interfaces around selected capabilities.
Constraints & planning

Organizational flexibility must account for clear responsibilities and appropriate access to HR information. Planning considers data consistency, access control and uptime; detailed internal rules and implementation remain private.
Delivered Capability

External applications were integrated through APIs built around existing service capabilities. Authentication and permission checks restricted access to sensitive HRMS records and protected workflows.
Technical approach
Full-stack web development with Google Cloud and Microsoft 365.
